title: The business idea
blurb: A concept in four parts, a feasibility check and a survey that tells you something.

levels.title: The concept in four parts
learn: Name the four parts of a business concept.
Tell a strong concept statement from a weak one.

cards.text: A business concept is a short, clear description of a business idea. It answers four questions. What is the product or service? Who is the customer? What is the benefit? How does the customer get it?

The product or service is what you sell. The customer is who buys it. The person who uses it is not always the person who pays. A club selling art kits to Grade 4 students has two people to think about: the child who uses the kit and the parent who pays.

A feature describes the product. A benefit is what the product does about the customer's problem. Customers buy benefits. Here are three features and benefits for hot chocolate sold at a winter market.

figure.title: Features and benefits
rows: Warms you up while you wait
Does not spill in your bag

cards.text: Distribution is how the product gets to the customer: where and when. A cart by the main doors at 3:15 reaches students who are waiting for the bus. A table in a quiet hallway at 9:00 reaches far fewer of them.

Bus Stop Cocoa sells hot chocolate in lidded cups to students waiting for the bus, so they warm up before the ride home. A cart by the main doors serves them from 3:15 to 3:45. The table pulls the statement apart.

figure.title: Bus Stop Cocoa, pulled apart
rows: A cart by the main doors, 3:15 to 3:45

cards.text: A weak statement: "We are selling cups. They come in red and blue. They will be on sale." It lists features. It names no customer, no benefit and no way to reach anyone. A good statement is two to four sentences with no bullet points, and it sounds clear read out loud.

questions.label: Four questions
questions.prompt: Which list gives the four questions a business concept answers?
questions.hint: Think of who, what, why it matters and how it gets there.

terms.meaning: A short, clear description of a business idea that answers four questions.

options.text: Product, price, place, promotion
options.why: Those are the 4 Ps of the marketing mix, a different tool. A concept asks about the customer and the benefit.

options.text: Product or service, customer, benefit, distribution
options.why: A concept answers all four of these, and it says them in a short statement.

options.text: Cost, price, profit, break-even
options.why: Those are money words. A concept describes the idea before it counts the money.

questions.label: Spot the benefit
questions.prompt: Priya sells study notes to Grade 9 students. Which line is a benefit rather than a feature?
questions.hint: A benefit is about what the customer gets done.

terms.meaning: Something true about the product itself, such as its size, colour or what it is made of.
What the product does about the customer's problem.

options.text: You can review a unit in ten minutes the night before
options.why: It is about the customer's problem: little time before a test.

options.text: The notes are typed in two colours
options.why: Colours are a feature. They describe the notes, not what the student gets done.

options.text: Each set of notes is four pages long
options.why: Length is a feature. It describes the product, not the customer's problem.

questions.label: Who pays
questions.prompt: A club sells a reading-buddy hour to kindergarten children. Parents book it and pay. Which sentence describes the two people correctly?
questions.hint: Ask who uses it and who pays.

options.text: The parent uses it and the child pays
options.why: It is the other way round. A kindergarten child is not the one who pays.

options.text: Only the child matters, because only the child uses it
options.why: The one who pays also decides. A club that ignores the parent loses the sale.

options.text: The child uses it and the parent pays
options.why: The child gets the hour. The parent decides to pay, so the club must win the parent too.

questions.label: Distribution phrase
questions.prompt: Which phrase answers "How does the customer get it?" for a hot lunch cart?
questions.hint: Look for where and when.

options.text: Soft rolls made with real butter
options.why: That is a feature. It says what the product is made of.

options.text: A cart by the gym doors from 12:00 to 12:20
options.why: It says where and when the customer gets the product.

options.text: Students who stay at school for lunch
options.why: That names the customer, not how the customer gets the product.

questions.label: Missing part
questions.prompt: Lantern Notes sells study guides to Grade 9 students, so they can review a unit in ten minutes before a test. Which of the four parts is missing?
questions.hint: Check each of the four questions against the sentence.

options.text: What is sold (the product)
options.why: It is there: study guides.

options.text: Who buys it (the customer)
options.why: It is there: Grade 9 students.

options.text: What the customer gains (the benefit)
options.why: It is there: a unit reviewed in ten minutes before a test.

options.text: How the customer gets it (distribution)
options.why: The sentence never says where or when students get the guides.

questions.label: Strongest statement
questions.prompt: Which concept statement is the strongest?
questions.hint: Look for a customer, a benefit and a way to reach them.

options.text: Felt Friends sells bookmarks to Grade 7 students needing a small gift, at a library table at lunch.
options.why: It names the product, the customer, the benefit and where they get it.

options.text: We sell bookmarks. They are made of felt. They come in six shapes.
options.why: Three features and nothing else. No customer, no benefit and no way to reach anyone.

options.text: Felt Friends will sell many different things to many different people.
options.why: Too wide. It names no customer, no benefit and no way to reach them.

questions.label: Name the customer
questions.prompt: Pocket Planner sells week-planner pages to Grade 10 students who forget deadlines, so nothing sneaks up on them. Pages are sold in the hallway on Monday mornings. Who is the customer?
questions.hint: Find who the pages are for.

options.text: Nobody in particular
options.why: The statement does name a group of students.

options.text: Students in the hallway on Mondays
options.why: That is where and when they are reached (distribution), not who the customer is.

options.text: Grade 10 students who forget deadlines
options.why: That is who the statement says will buy and use the pages.

questions.label: Feature to benefit
questions.prompt: The feature is "Our lamps are solar-powered." Which line turns it into a benefit?
questions.hint: A benefit says what the customer gains.

terms.meaning: Something true about the product itself, such as its size, colour or what it is made of.
What the product does about the customer's problem.

options.text: Our lamps are very well made
options.why: That is a general claim. It names no gain for the customer.

options.text: The lights stay on at camp with no batteries to buy
options.why: It says what the customer gains from the feature.

options.text: Our lamps come in three colours
options.why: That is another feature. It describes the product only.

questions.label: Statement format
questions.prompt: Which format is right for a concept statement?
questions.hint: It should sound clear when read out loud.

options.text: Two to four sentences that read well out loud
options.why: That is the format. After one listen, a classmate should name the customer and the benefit.

options.text: A bullet list of every feature
options.why: A list of features is what a weak statement looks like.

options.text: One long page with all the detail
options.why: Too long to say out loud. A concept is short and clear.

levels.title: Feasibility and the competition
learn: Check whether an idea has a market you can reach.
Read a competitive matrix and name why you win.

cards.text: Feasibility asks whether an idea can work, and it needs evidence. It has three questions. Is there a market? Can you reach it? Why would people pick you over the others?

A market is not the whole school. It is the people in the right place, at the right time, with the right need and money. Oakfield School has 800 students. 70% stay for lunch. Half of those buy anything. A quarter of those would buy a hot drink.

The honest market must be bigger than the break-even point: the number of items a business must sell for its sales to cover all of its costs. The next unit works it out. If a stand needs 90 sales and its honest market is 70 students, the plan is short of buyers.

Where and when you sell changes who you reach: the lunch line, between classes, after school or at an event. Each has different customers, a different amount of time to buy and different money in their pockets. Sell where your customer already is.

A direct competitor sells the same thing to the same customer. An indirect competitor wins the same dollar another way. Doing nothing is a competitor too, because many students just buy nothing. You win for one honest reason: cheaper, closer, better or different.

A competitive matrix lists competitors side by side with a strength and a weakness for each. Here is the one for Bus Stop Cocoa, which charges $2.00. A team then writes one reason to win for each row, including the row for doing nothing.

questions.label: Reach question
questions.prompt: Which feasibility question is about where and when you sell?
questions.hint: There are three questions: market, reach, win.

options.text: Is there a market?
options.why: That asks whether enough customers exist, not where you meet them.

options.text: Why would people pick you?
options.why: That asks why you beat the others, not where you sell.

options.text: Can you reach them?
options.why: Reach is about getting in front of the customer at the right place and time.

questions.label: Closest market
questions.prompt: Bus Stop Cocoa's customer is students waiting for the bus. Which group is closest to its honest market?
questions.hint: The market is the right people, at the right time, with money.

terms.meaning: The people who are in the right place, at the right time, with the right need and money.

options.text: Students at the bus stop who would buy a hot drink
options.why: It is the right people in the right place who want it.

options.text: Every student in the school
options.why: Most of them are not at the stop at that time or would not buy.

options.text: Everyone who has ever bought a drink
options.why: That ignores the place, the time and the hot drink.

questions.label: Share who buy
questions.prompt: Ravi's school has 600 students. Half stay at school for lunch. Of those, 40% buy a snack. What percent of all 600 students buy a snack at lunch?
questions.hint: Find the number who stay first, then the number of those who buy.
questions.why: Each step keeps a share of the step before. Of all students, 20% buy a snack at lunch.
questions.miss: Take 40% of the students who stay, not of the whole school, then compare with the whole school.

traps.why: That adds 50% and 40%. Each step takes a share of the step before.
That is only the share of those who stayed. Compare the buyers with all the students.

questions.label: Share for hot food
questions.prompt: Tia's school has 500 students. 60% stay at school for lunch. Of those, 1 in 5 would buy hot food. What percent of all 500 students is that?
questions.hint: Take 1 in 5 of the students who stay, then compare with all of them.
questions.why: The buyers are 1 in 5 of the students who stay, which is 12% of the whole school.
questions.miss: Work out how many stay, take 1 in 5 of that number, then compare with all the students.

traps.why: That adds 60% and 20%. The 20% applies to the students who stay, not to everyone.
That is the share of those who stay. Compare with all the students at the school.

questions.label: Market and break-even
questions.prompt: A stand must sell 120 cups to break even. Its honest market is 90 students, each buying at most one cup. What does that show?
questions.hint: Compare the number the stand needs with the number who could buy.

terms.meaning: The number of items a business must sell for its sales to cover all of its costs.

options.text: The plan works, because 90 is a big number
options.why: Size on its own does not decide it. The market must be bigger than the break-even.

options.text: The market is smaller than the break-even, so the plan must change
options.why: It needs 120 buyers and only 90 exist, so the plan is short of buyers.

options.text: The market will grow once students hear about it
options.why: That is a guess. The honest market is the number you can show.

questions.label: Direct competitor
questions.prompt: Which is a direct competitor of a hot chocolate stand at a school winter market?
questions.hint: Same thing, same customer.

terms.meaning: A business that sells the same thing to the same customer.

options.text: A vending machine with cold drinks
options.why: It wins the same dollar a different way, so it is an indirect competitor.

options.text: Another club's hot chocolate table
options.why: It sells the same thing to the same customers.

options.text: A student who brings water from home
options.why: That student buys nothing, so this is doing nothing.

questions.label: Doing nothing
questions.prompt: At 3:15 most students buy nothing at all. Which competitor is that?
questions.hint: Nothing is being sold by this competitor.

options.text: Doing nothing
options.why: Not buying is a competitor too, and it never appears on a list.

options.text: A direct competitor
options.why: A direct competitor sells the same thing. These students buy nothing.

options.text: An indirect competitor
options.why: An indirect competitor sells something else for the same dollar. Here nothing is sold.

questions.label: Reason to win
questions.prompt: Bus Stop Cocoa's cart is at the main doors. The corner shop is ten minutes away. Which reason to win does the distance show?
questions.hint: Think about where they already are.

options.text: Cheaper
options.why: Price is a different reason. The distance is about location.

options.text: Different
options.why: Different means nobody else offers it. The corner shop sells drinks too.

options.text: Closer
options.why: The cart is where the students already are.

questions.label: A real reason
questions.prompt: Which "why we win" is a real reason with a reason attached?
questions.hint: Pick one of the four reasons and say why.

options.text: Ours is good and everyone likes it
options.why: That is not one of the four honest reasons, and it gives no evidence.

options.text: Closer: our cart is at the door they leave by
options.why: It names one of the four reasons and gives evidence for it.

options.text: We worked very hard on it all week
options.why: Effort is not a reason a customer picks you.

questions.label: Cheaper than $2.50
questions.prompt: A new juice stand will charge $2.50. Tap the competitor that already charges less than that.
questions.hint: Read the price on each bar.

figure.title: Price of one bottle of juice

questions.miss: Compare each bar with $2.50. Only one is lower.

levels.title: A survey that tells you something
learn: Write survey questions that get evidence.

cards.text: A survey asks many people a few short questions. Opinions are cheap and polite. Evidence is what a person did, with a number. A survey that gathers opinions mostly tells you people are being nice.

figure.title: Opinion or evidence
rows: I take the bus four days a week
I paid $4 for one at a market

cards.text: Rule 1: ask about the past, not the future. People are poor at predicting what they will do and good at saying what they did. Ask about last week, not next month.

figure.title: Ask about the past
rows: Would you buy a hot drink after school?
When did you last buy a hot drink at school?

cards.text: Rule 2: do not lead. A leading question hints at the answer the asker wants: "Don't you think the vending machine is too dear?" Ask "What do you usually spend at the vending machine?" Offer real choices, so people pick instead of agreeing.

Rule 3: one thing per question. "Would you buy a cheap, warm, healthy snack?" asks three things. A "no" does not say which one. Rule 4: keep it quick. About five questions, mostly multiple choice, and at most one open box.

A short survey needs five answers: do they buy at all, how much do they spend, would they pick you over real alternatives, what price, and what would stop them. For price, offer a choice of prices with a "would not buy" option, because people say they would pay more than they do.

Bus Stop Cocoa asked 40 classmates "When did you last buy a hot drink at school?" A share is a count divided by the total. 18 of 40 is 45%. These 40 know the team and share a class, so ask a few people outside the class too.

questions.label: Evidence or opinion
questions.prompt: Which answer is evidence rather than opinion?
questions.hint: Evidence is something a person did.

terms.meaning: A short set of questions asked to many people, to learn what they do and want.

options.text: I bought a hot drink twice last week
options.why: It says what the person did, with a number.

options.text: That sounds like a great idea
options.why: That is an opinion. It says nothing about what the person did.

options.text: I would probably buy one
options.why: That is a guess about the future, not something that happened.

questions.label: Ask the past
questions.prompt: Which question asks about the past?
questions.hint: Look for a time that has already happened.

options.text: How many gifts did you buy last month?
options.why: It asks what the person did, which they can answer from memory.

options.text: Would you buy a bracelet from us?
options.why: That asks about the future. It gets a polite guess.

options.text: Will you buy gifts next month?
options.why: That also asks about the future, and people predict badly.

questions.label: Leading question
questions.prompt: Which question is a leading question?
questions.hint: Which one hints at the answer wanted?

terms.meaning: A question that hints at the answer the asker wants.

options.text: What snack did you buy most last week?
options.why: It asks what happened and hints at no answer.

options.text: Which of these snacks did you buy most last week?
options.why: It gives real choices and does not push an answer.

options.text: Don't you agree our cookies are the best snack at school?
options.why: It pushes the student toward yes.

questions.label: Two at once
questions.prompt: Which question asks two things at once?
questions.hint: A "no" should always tell you what to change.

options.text: How much did you pay for your last hot drink?
options.why: That asks one thing.

options.text: Is our drink warm and cheap?
options.why: A "no" does not say whether the drink was not warm or not cheap.

options.text: When did you last buy a hot drink?
options.why: That asks one thing.

questions.label: Real alternatives
questions.prompt: One survey question asks students to pick between Bus Stop Cocoa and alternatives. Which set of options is best?
questions.hint: Use the competitors from a matrix.

options.text: Bus Stop Cocoa, the vending machine, the corner shop
options.why: These are real alternatives a student could pick instead.

options.text: Bus Stop Cocoa and two choices nobody would pick
options.why: Obviously worse options flatter you and prove nothing.

options.text: Bus Stop Cocoa only, yes or no
options.why: With no alternatives, agreeing costs the student nothing.

questions.label: Price question
questions.prompt: Which price question can show how many students would not buy at any of the prices?
questions.hint: Look for a way to say no to all the prices.

options.text: How much would you pay?
options.why: Everyone names a price and people say they would pay more than they do.

options.text: Would you pay $3 for this?
options.why: A yes or no on one price tells you nothing about the other prices.

options.text: Which price would you pick: $2, $3, $4 or would not buy?
options.why: It forces a choice between prices and allows "would not buy".

questions.label: Would not buy
questions.prompt: Dev's team asked 50 students to pick a price. The table shows the answers. What percent chose "Would not buy"?
questions.hint: Divide that count by the total number of students asked.
questions.why: 14 of 50 chose "Would not buy", which is 28%.
questions.miss: Divide by the total of all four rows, not by one row.

traps.why: That is the count. A share is the count divided by the total asked.
That is the share who picked a price. The question asks about "Would not buy".

questions.label: Picked $3 or $4
questions.prompt: Using the same table, what percent of the students picked $3 or $4?
questions.hint: Add the two counts first.
questions.miss: Add the counts for the two prices, then divide by all students asked.

traps.why: That is the count. A share is the count divided by the total asked.
That is everyone who did not pick $3 or $4.

questions.label: Outside answers
questions.prompt: Mei's team got 28 answers from classmates and 7 from people outside the class. What percent of all the answers came from outside the class?
questions.hint: Add the answers first to get the total.
questions.why: 7 of 35 answers came from outside, which is 20%.
questions.miss: The total is every answer, from the class and from outside it.

traps.why: That divides by the 28 classmates. The total must include all answers.
That is the count. A share is the count divided by the total.

questions.label: Reading friends
questions.prompt: A team asked 30 friends in its own class "Would you buy this? Yes or no" and 27 said yes. What is the right way to read that?
questions.hint: Think about who answered and what kind of answer it is.

options.text: Opinion from friends in one class; it does not show the market
options.why: The answers are guesses from friends, not what buyers did.

options.text: Strong evidence that most students will buy
options.why: A guess from friends is not evidence about the whole market.

options.text: Proof that the price is right
options.why: The question did not ask about price at all.
